subject: film
title: Cinema Novo: Brazil's cinema of hunger, 1960 to 1972
dek: In the early 1960s a group of young Brazilian directors, most of them in their twenties, decided that their country's films should stop copying Hollywood and start showing Brazil as it was: the drought-stricken northeast, the favelas of Rio, the hungry and the powerless. With little money and handheld cameras they made some of the most important political films of the century. Then a military coup in 1964, and a harsher crackdown in 1968, forced the movement to change shape, turn to allegory and finally scatter.
era: c. 1960 to 1972, with roots in the mid-1950s
honesty: This lesson keeps to facts documented in the English and Portuguese Wikipedia articles on Cinema Novo, its directors and its main films, and the sources they cite. Where a famous story is only weakly sourced, the lesson says so. Film years follow the most common release dates. There are no images today rather than risk pictures that do not match their captions.

timeline.label: Atlântida opens in Rio
timeline.detail: The Atlântida studio is founded in Rio de Janeiro. Its cheap, popular musical comedies, called chanchadas, dominate Brazilian screens until the mid-1950s.

timeline.label: Vera Cruz is founded
timeline.detail: Industrialists in São Paulo set up the Vera Cruz studio to make polished, Hollywood-style films. It hires Alberto Cavalcanti and many foreign technicians.

timeline.label: Vera Cruz collapses
timeline.detail: Despite international success with O Cangaceiro (1953), the studio stops production after only five years, deep in debt.

timeline.label: Rio, 40 Graus
timeline.detail: Nelson Pereira dos Santos releases his first feature, a neorealist day in the life of five favela boys. It is later seen as the movement's starting point.

timeline.label: Cinco Vezes Favela
timeline.detail: The students' Popular Culture Centre produces a five-part film about Rio's favelas, with segments by Cacá Diegues, Joaquim Pedro de Andrade and Leon Hirszman.

timeline.label: Barren Lives
timeline.detail: Nelson Pereira dos Santos adapts Graciliano Ramos's novel about a starving family in the northeast. It competes at Cannes the next year.

timeline.label: Black God, White Devil and the coup
timeline.detail: Glauber Rocha's film and Ruy Guerra's The Guns appear. On 31 March to 1 April the army overthrows President João Goulart.

timeline.label: An Aesthetic of Hunger
timeline.detail: Rocha publishes his manifesto arguing that hunger is the essence of Latin American society and the source of its cinema's originality.

timeline.label: Entranced Earth
timeline.detail: Rocha's film about a poet caught between a dictator and a populist is banned, then released after protests. It wins the critics' prize at Cannes.

timeline.label: AI-5
timeline.detail: On 13 December the military government issues Institutional Act Number 5, closing Congress and tightening censorship.

timeline.label: Macunaíma and Antonio das Mortes
timeline.detail: Joaquim Pedro de Andrade's comic Macunaíma becomes a hit. Rocha wins Best Director at Cannes. The state creates Embrafilme.

timeline.label: How Tasty Was My Little Frenchman
timeline.detail: Nelson Pereira dos Santos makes a black comedy about cannibalism with dialogue almost entirely in Tupi. Rocha goes into exile around this time.

timeline.label: Rocha dies
timeline.detail: Glauber Rocha dies in Rio de Janeiro at 42.

fun_fact.title: Too hot to be true
fun_fact.text: Nelson Pereira dos Santos's Rio, 40 Graus (1955), the film usually named as Cinema Novo's starting point, was banned for a time soon after it was finished. A story repeated ever since, though not well documented, says the Rio police chief who acted as censor objected to the title itself, claiming the city's average temperature had never gone above 39.6 degrees. Writers and filmmakers campaigned against the ban, and the film was released.

sections.title: Before Cinema Novo: carnival comedies and a failed Hollywood

blocks.text: In the 1940s and early 1950s, most Brazilian films that ordinary people saw were chanchadas. These were cheap, fast musical comedies, many of them made by the Atlântida studio in Rio de Janeiro, which opened in 1941. They were full of carnival songs, mistaken identities and parodies of Hollywood hits, and they made stars of comedians such as Oscarito and Grande Otelo. Audiences loved them. Critics and young intellectuals tended to see them as silly and as proof that Brazil could only imitate foreign films badly.

In 1949 a group of São Paulo industrialists, led by the Italian-born producer Franco Zampari and Francisco Matarazzo Sobrinho, tried a different route. They founded the Vera Cruz studio in São Bernardo do Campo and hired the Brazilian director Alberto Cavalcanti, who had built his career in France and Britain, to run it. Vera Cruz imported foreign technicians and aimed for the polish of a Hollywood studio. It produced more than forty features, and one of them, Lima Barreto's bandit film O Cangaceiro (1953), won a prize at Cannes. But the costs were too high for the Brazilian market, distribution was controlled by others, and the company stopped production in 1954.

For the young cinephiles who would start Cinema Novo, both models had failed. The chanchada was popular but, in their view, empty. Vera Cruz was serious but expensive and foreign in spirit. They found a third model in Italian neorealism, which had shown after the war that a poor country could make great films on real streets with non-professional actors. Nelson Pereira dos Santos applied that lesson in Rio, 40 Graus (1955), which follows five boys from a favela who sell peanuts around Copacabana, Sugarloaf Mountain and the Maracanã stadium on a hot Sunday. He followed it with Rio, Zona Norte (1957). Many of the younger directors came to see him as the movement's father.

The wider country was also changing fast. In the late 1950s, under President Juscelino Kubitschek, Brazil was building Brasília and promising 'fifty years of progress in five'. At the same time, millions of people in the northeast lived in extreme poverty, and peasant leagues were organising for land reform. Bossa nova was giving Brazilian music a modern, international sound. Young people in the student movement believed that art should help the country understand itself, and many expected real political change soon.

sections.title: A camera in hand and an idea in the head

blocks.text: Cinema Novo means simply 'new cinema'. It was a loose group of friends and rivals rather than a school with rules, and its members disagreed often. Its most famous slogan, usually credited to Glauber Rocha, was 'a camera in hand and an idea in the head'. The point was that a filmmaker did not need a studio, stars or a big budget. What mattered was having something urgent to say about Brazil and the will to go out and film it.

items: Real places and real poverty. The films went to the sertão, the dry backlands of the northeast, and to the favelas of Rio, places that commercial cinema mostly ignored.

Low budgets and visible roughness. Handheld cameras, harsh natural light and rough editing were not hidden. The directors argued that a poor country's cinema should look like the conditions it came from.
Politics. Most of the directors were on the left. Their films dealt with landowners and peasants, hunger, religious fanaticism, bandits, populist politicians and the failures of the middle class.
Brazilian culture as raw material. Films drew on folk ballads, popular religion, carnival, Afro-Brazilian history and Brazilian modernist literature instead of Hollywood genres.
Authorship. Like the French New Wave, Cinema Novo believed the director was the author of the film, and each director had a strong personal style.

blocks.text: Historians usually divide the movement into three phases. The first, from about 1960 to 1964, focused on the rural poor and the sertão and was full of hope that cinema could help bring revolution. The second, from the coup of 1964 to about 1968, turned to the failures of intellectuals and the middle class, and to how the left had lost. The third, from about 1968 to 1972, after censorship tightened, turned to colourful allegory, comedy and what was called the cannibal or tropicalist style.

The movement's central theory came from Rocha's 1965 manifesto, An Aesthetic of Hunger. He wrote that the hunger of Latin America is not simply an alarming symptom but the essence of its society, and that Cinema Novo's originality was this hunger. He argued that European audiences liked Latin American misery as an exotic subject but did not understand it, and that the only honest response to hunger was a cinema that was itself hungry, rough and even violent in form. The essay became one of the founding texts of political cinema across the developing world.

Glauber Rocha (1939 to 1981) was the movement's leader, theorist and loudest voice. He came from Vitória da Conquista in Bahia, worked as a film critic as a teenager, and made his first feature, Barravento (1962), about a fishing village and its Afro-Brazilian religious traditions, in his early twenties. His great films are Black God, White Devil (1964), Entranced Earth (1967) and Antonio das Mortes (1969), which won him the Best Director prize at Cannes. He was famous for big statements; he once said, echoing Louis XIV, 'I am the Cinema Novo'.

Nelson Pereira dos Santos (1928 to 2018) was older and calmer. After his two Rio films he made Barren Lives (Vidas Secas, 1963), based on Graciliano Ramos's 1938 novel. It follows a family of drifters, the cowherd Fabiano, his wife, their two sons and their dog, Baleia, as they flee drought across the northeast in the 1940s. The cinematographer Luiz Carlos Barreto shot it in a hard, white light that makes the heat almost physical. The film was shown in competition at Cannes in 1964 and is often called the most perfect film of the movement. Later he made the black comedy How Tasty Was My Little Frenchman (1971).

Ruy Guerra, born in Mozambique when it was a Portuguese colony, made The Guns (Os Fuzis, 1964). Soldiers are sent to a drought-stricken town in the sertão to stop starving people from looting a food warehouse owned by the mayor, while pilgrims follow an ox they believe is holy. The film won a Silver Bear at the Berlin festival in 1964.

Carlos 'Cacá' Diegues made Ganga Zumba (1963), about enslaved Africans escaping to the runaway settlement of Palmares in the seventeenth century, one of the first Brazilian films centred on Black history. He later made popular hits such as Xica da Silva (1976) and Bye Bye Brasil (1980). Joaquim Pedro de Andrade began with documentaries, including Garrincha, Alegria do Povo (1962) about the football star, and later made Macunaíma (1969). Leon Hirszman made the favela segment Pedreira de São Diogo, the colour film Garota de Ipanema (1968), São Bernardo (1972) and, much later, They Don't Wear Black Tie (1981). Paulo César Saraceni made Porto das Caixas (1962) and The Challenge (O Desafio, 1965), one of the first films about intellectuals after the coup.

An important early collective work was Cinco Vezes Favela (1962), five short films about Rio's favelas produced by the Popular Culture Centre of the National Union of Students. Its directors included Diegues, Joaquim Pedro de Andrade and Hirszman. The same year, Anselmo Duarte's The Given Word (O Pagador de Promessas, 1962), about a poor man who tries to carry a cross into a church in Salvador, won the Palme d'Or at Cannes. Duarte was not part of the Cinema Novo group, but the prize showed the world that serious Brazilian films about the poor could compete with the best.

sections.title: Black God, White Devil: the sertão will become the sea

blocks.text: Black God, White Devil (Deus e o Diabo na Terra do Sol, 1964; the Portuguese title means 'God and the Devil in the Land of the Sun') is Rocha's most famous film and the classic of the first phase. Manoel, a poor cowherd in the sertão, kills the landowner who cheats him out of his share of cattle. With his wife Rosa he flees and joins Sebastião, a preacher who promises his followers that the dry backlands will turn into sea and the sea into land. When the preacher's religious fanaticism ends in a child sacrifice, Manoel turns instead to Corisco, a cangaceiro, or bandit, who survives his famous leader Lampião and wants revenge on the rich. Hunting them both is Antônio das Mortes, a hired killer paid by landowners and the Church.

The film draws on real history. Messianic movements had appeared many times in the sertão, most famously at Canudos in the 1890s, and the cangaceiros were real outlaws of the 1920s and 1930s. Rocha tells the story like a folk ballad, with a singer narrating on the soundtrack, mixed with music by Heitor Villa-Lobos. The camera is handheld and the light is blinding. Some scenes are long and static, and others explode into sudden violence.

The film's argument is that neither religion nor banditry can save the poor, because both are blind reactions to oppression rather than conscious politics. In the final scene Manoel runs across the dry land, and the image cuts to the sea, as a song repeats that the sertão will become the sea. Many viewers read it as a call for revolution. The film was completed just before the coup of 1964 and competed at Cannes in May of that year. To the military government that had just taken power, it was exactly the kind of film it distrusted.

sections.title: After the coup: Entranced Earth and the defeated poet

blocks.text: On 31 March and 1 April 1964 the army removed the elected president, João Goulart, who had promised land reform and was accused by his opponents of moving toward communism. The generals said they would hold power briefly. They stayed until 1985. For the Cinema Novo directors, who had expected their country to move left, it was a shock. Their films had been made for 'the people', but the people had not risen to defend the government, and the films themselves had mostly been seen by students and art-house audiences.

Rocha's answer was Entranced Earth (Terra em Transe, 1967). It is set in Eldorado, an imaginary Latin American country. The poet and journalist Paulo Martins drifts between a conservative, almost mystical politician, Porfírio Díaz, and a populist provincial governor, Vieira, who speaks for the poor but backs down when real conflict comes. In the end Díaz takes power in a coup, and Paulo, dying, is left with nothing but his rage. In one famous scene Paulo covers the mouth of a union leader to stop him speaking, a bitter image of intellectuals who claim to speak for the people without letting them speak.

The film was a self-portrait of the left-wing intellectual and a harsh one. Censors banned it in April 1967 for tarnishing Brazil's image. After protests from filmmakers in Brazil and France, the government allowed it to be shown, and it won the international critics' prize at Cannes in 1967. It had a strong effect on young artists at home. The singer Caetano Veloso later said that seeing it was a turning point for him, and the music movement he and Gilberto Gil launched in 1967 and 1968, Tropicália, shared its chaotic, satirical mix of high and low culture.

sections.title: Cannibals and tropicalism: AI-5 and allegory

blocks.text: On 13 December 1968 the military government issued Institutional Act Number 5, known as AI-5. It closed Congress, suspended habeas corpus for political crimes and greatly expanded censorship. Arrests, torture and exile became common. Gilberto Gil and Caetano Veloso were arrested at the end of that month and later left for London. Openly political films became almost impossible to make.

The directors turned to allegory and comedy. They took inspiration from the modernist writer Oswald de Andrade, whose Cannibalist Manifesto (1928) had argued that Brazilian culture should 'eat' foreign influences and turn them into something new, as the Tupi people were said to eat their enemies. Joaquim Pedro de Andrade's Macunaíma (1969), based on Mário de Andrade's 1928 novel, follows a lazy, greedy and very funny 'hero without any character' who is born Black in the jungle, played by the chanchada star Grande Otelo, turns white, and travels to São Paulo. It was a box-office success, and it showed that Cinema Novo could reach a mass audience by borrowing the colour and humour of the chanchada it had once despised.

Nelson Pereira dos Santos's How Tasty Was My Little Frenchman (1971) is set in the sixteenth century, when French and Portuguese colonists were fighting over the coast of Brazil. A Frenchman is captured by the Tupinambá, who take him for Portuguese. He lives among them, learns their ways and takes a wife, and is then ritually killed and eaten. Almost all the dialogue is in Tupi, and the actors wear historically accurate costume, which means a great deal of nudity. The film quotes European travel writers of the time ironically and turns the colonial story upside down.

Rocha's Antonio das Mortes (1969) brought back the hired killer of Black God, White Devil, now in colour, and showed him changing sides to fight for the poor. It won the Best Director prize at Cannes. Rocha soon left Brazil and made films abroad, including in the Congo and Spain. In 1969 the government created Embrafilme, a state film company, which in the 1970s funded and distributed many Brazilian films, including later works by Cinema Novo directors. That support came from the same regime that censored them, a contradiction critics have argued about ever since.

A younger group reacted against Cinema Novo in the late 1960s. Directors of what was called Cinema Marginal, such as Rogério Sganzerla with The Red Light Bandit (O Bandido da Luz Vermelha, 1968) and Júlio Bressane, made even cheaper, wilder and more anarchic films. They saw Cinema Novo as having become an establishment.

sections.title: What was happening elsewhere at the same time

blocks.text: Cinema Novo was part of a wave of political filmmaking across Latin America. In Cuba, the revolutionary government founded the film institute ICAIC in 1959, and Tomás Gutiérrez Alea made Memories of Underdevelopment (1968). In Argentina, Fernando Solanas and Octavio Getino made the long documentary The Hour of the Furnaces (1968) and in 1969 wrote the manifesto Towards a Third Cinema, which called for a cinema of liberation that was neither Hollywood entertainment nor European art cinema. In Bolivia, Jorge Sanjinés made Blood of the Condor (1969). Rocha's essay on hunger was one of the texts these filmmakers read and argued with.

In Africa, the Senegalese writer and director Ousmane Sembène made Black Girl (1966), and Gillo Pontecorvo's The Battle of Algiers (1966) showed the Algerian war of independence in a newsreel style. In Europe, the French New Wave and the Czechoslovak New Wave were at their height, and Cinema Novo directors knew the French critics and festivals well. The same years saw new waves in Japan and in New Hollywood. What set Cinema Novo apart was its insistence on hunger and underdevelopment as the subject and the style of its films.

In Taiwan at the same time, the state-run Central Motion Picture Corporation chose a very different kind of realism. In 1963 its general manager, Gong Hong, launched the policy of 'healthy realism', which set stories among farmers and fishing families but emphasised hard work, kindness and progress under the government. Oyster Girl (1964), directed by Li Jia and Li Hsing, about a young woman in an oyster-farming village on the west coast, won Best Feature Film at the 1964 Asian Film Festival. Both movements took inspiration from Italian neorealism and filmed the rural poor, but Cinema Novo used poverty to criticise the state, while healthy realism showed poverty being overcome with the state's help. Taiwan's own critical realism would come later, with Taiwan New Cinema in the 1980s.

By the early 1970s Cinema Novo had ended as a movement, though its directors kept working. Hirszman's They Don't Wear Black Tie (1981), about a strike in São Paulo, won a Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival. Diegues's Bye Bye Brasil (1980) followed a travelling circus across a country being changed by television and highways. Rocha returned to Brazil, made his last feature, The Age of the Earth (A Idade da Terra, 1980), and died in 1981 at 42.

The movement's influence is large. It gave Latin American cinema a theory and a confidence it had not had before, and it shaped Third Cinema across the developing world. Later Brazilian films about poverty and violence, such as City of God (2002), are often compared with it, sometimes unfavourably, because critics argue that they turned hunger into slick spectacle, the very thing Rocha had warned against. Cinema Novo also showed something that other lessons in this course return to: from Italian neorealism to Taiwan New Cinema, a country's first serious look at itself on screen often comes from young people with very little money and a strong sense that the official picture is false.

sections.title: A question to take with you

blocks.text: Rocha argued that a film about hunger should look hungry: rough, poor and uncomfortable. Macunaíma reached a huge audience by being colourful and funny instead. Which approach do you think does more to make an audience understand poverty, and can a film about suffering be beautiful without becoming a spectacle?
